title: Drain a house you can't heat, and keep its water
summary: When a house will freeze, save the water in the pipes and water heater, then drain everything and put RV (propylene glycol) antifreeze in the traps and toilets so nothing bursts. The dangers are scalding water heater water, lead in old pipes, car antifreeze, and thawing pipes with a flame.

materials.item: Clean containers for the saved water: jugs, pots, food-grade buckets with lids
RV or plumbing antifreeze labelled propylene glycol, never car antifreeze
materials.qty: at least 1 L of mix per trap and 4 L per toilet (mix as the label says)

materials.item: Short drinking-water-safe hose for the water heater drain
Blankets or insulation for pipes you can't drain
Sponge and rags for toilet bowls; towels for thawing
Tape and a marker for signs

steps.text: Decide early. If the house will fall below freezing, drain the plumbing before it freezes (Get Prepared outages, Manitoba Hydro). A warm room or a standby stove only counts if no pipe anywhere can freeze (Winter power failures).

While there is still pressure, fill every clean container you have: drinking water, cooking water and enough to mix antifreeze (WSC winterizing). Then close the main valve where the water enters; on a well, switch off the pump's own breaker and leave the main on (WSC winterizing).
steps.warn: Never feed the pump from a generator through a wall outlet; only through an approved transfer panel (Get Prepared outages). Run the generator outdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from any building (Get Prepared outages): its exhaust is carbon monoxide.

steps.text: Turn off the water heater: electric at its breaker (Bradford White); gas by putting the pilot out (Winter power failures).
steps.warn: Electric elements burn out if powered while the tank isn't full (Bradford White). Tape the breaker off and label it. Never turn on the gas or power to a heater with an empty tank (FEMA 2004, OSU BAE-1519).

steps.text: Collect the pipe water: open the highest tap in the house to let air in, then draw water off the lowest tap or the basement drain valve into clean containers (FEMA 2004, Winter power failures).
steps.warn: In a house with lead pipe (to 1975) or lead solder (to 1986), this standing water carries more lead the longer it has sat (EPA lead). Wash with it (skin doesn't absorb lead from water, EPA lead); keep it out of children's and babies' drinks and formula (Health Canada lead).

steps.text: When the water heater has cooled, close its cold inlet valve, open the drain valve at the bottom into clean pots, and open a hot tap to let air in (Bradford White).
steps.warn: Canadian electric heaters are set to 60 °C (140 °F), which scalds in 5 seconds (Bradford White), and a switched-off tank is still full of hot water (WSC winterizing). A garden hose can add lead (Cleveland Water hose).

steps.text: Floor by floor from the top, open every hot and cold tap, tub and shower, and flush each toilet so its tank empties (Winter power failures, WSC winterizing). For an outside tap, close its inside shut-off, then open the outside tap (WSC pipes). Leave the basement drain valve open (Winter power failures).

Unhook and drain the washing machine hoses, and siphon or drain its tub into the floor drain (Winter power failures, WSC winterizing). Drain the dishwasher, the fridge ice-maker line and any furnace humidifier (Purdue PrepNote).

On a well, drain the pressure tank (Purdue PrepNote) and leave the pump's wiring alone unless you can prove it dead. With the breaker off and taped, test the wires with a meter first; then disconnecting the wiring is a second guard (WSC winterizing). A pump in a deep well you can't reach won't freeze; drain an above-ground jet pump over a bucket (WSC winterizing). Lay a water softener's resin tank on its side to drain (Purdue PrepNote).
steps.warn: Submersible pump motors are standard at 230 V, more than one disconnect may feed them, and some controls hold a lethal charge for 5 minutes after the power is off (Franklin AIM).

steps.text: Hot-water heating: keep the circulator running while you have power; drain once rooms drop below about 4 °C (40 °F) (Purdue PrepNote). Turn off the boiler's switch, fuel and water feed (Weil-McLain WGO), open its drain into the floor drain, and open a top-floor radiator vent (WSC winterizing).
steps.warn: Let a hot boiler cool first, and never add cold water to a hot one: it can crack (Weil-McLain WGO). Boiler and radiator water is never for drinking (FEMA FAQ); CDC says to use the tap water heater tank, not the heating system tank (CDC find water).

steps.text: Blow remaining water out of each tap with low-pressure air if you have a compressor (WSC winterizing); a little left in level pipes doesn't matter (Winter power failures). Wrap pipes you can't drain, the main valve, the inlet pipe and the meter or pump in blankets or insulation (Winter power failures, Purdue PrepNote).

Pour RV antifreeze labelled propylene glycol slowly into every trap, mixed with water as the label directs for your coldest weather: at least 1 L (1 US qt) of the mix into each sink, basin and tub trap and about 1 L into the main house trap (WSC winterizing). Purdue PrepNote says as much as the trap holds, 0.5 to 1 L, and lists showers, washtubs and floor drains to check too.
steps.warn: Never car antifreeze (ethylene glycol): it isn't safe anywhere in a home water system (Purdue PrepNote). Ethanol RV antifreeze is flammable (Prestone SDS 834).

steps.text: Toilets: with the tank empty, sponge the bowl dry, pour at least 4 L (1 US gal) of mixed antifreeze into the tank and flush so it settles in the bowl's trap (WSC winterizing).
Tape a sign on every tap, toilet and the pump switch so nobody turns them on (WSC winterizing). Use a bucket toilet from now on.

If a pipe froze before you drained it, open its tap and warm the pipe with towels soaked in hot water, starting near the tap and working towards the coldest part (Winnipeg thaw, ICC winter water). If it leaks, close the main valve (Winnipeg thaw).
steps.warn: No torch or open flame, ever (ICC winter water, Winnipeg thaw, Simcoe Muskoka), and no boiling water: it can burst the pipe (Winnipeg thaw).

steps.text: To restore: close the drains, turn the supply on, close the lowest taps first and bleed air at the top, and fill the water heater before it gets power or gas (Winter power failures, FEMA 2004). On a hot-water boiler, refill the system to its correct pressure and bleed the radiator vents, lowest floor first, before you fire it (Weil-McLain WGO). Then run the hot tap several minutes (Bradford White).
steps.warn: After two weeks or more unused, a hot-water system can hold flammable hydrogen: no flame or smoking near the tap (Bradford White). Never fire a boiler without water: it overheats and is damaged (Weil-McLain WGO).

notes:
## When to drain

A federal winter-outage guide calls the plumbing the main threat when a house goes cold, and says that if you heat with a standby stove you still have to check that no part of the plumbing can freeze (Winter power failures). If the house is going to drop below freezing, drain the water out of the plumbing before it freezes (Get Prepared outages, Manitoba Hydro). One warm room ([Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm)) doesn't keep pipes in outside walls or a cold basement thawed.

You still need water to drink and wash: store it first (next section), then use a bucket toilet ([Toilets in winter](#guides/skill_toilets_in_winter)) once the toilets hold antifreeze.

## Save the water first

Before you open a single drain:
- Fill every clean container you have from the taps while there is still pressure. Set aside drinking and cooking water, plus enough to mix any antifreeze (WSC winterizing).
- Shut the main valve where the water comes in. That also stops dirty water from a failing town main getting into your pipes (CDC find water).
- Then let air in at the highest tap in the house and draw water off the lowest tap into clean pots and jugs (FEMA 2004, OSU BAE-1519).
- The water heater holds a lot: the electric models in one maker's manual run from 19 to 119 US gal (72 to 450 L) (Bradford White). Heater and pipe water are drinking water if the supply was safe (FEMA FAQ, FEMA 2004); boil or disinfect it if unsure (CDC water safe). Never take boiler or radiator water (FEMA FAQ); CDC likewise says to use the tap water heater tank, not the heating system tank (CDC find water). More in [Water in buildings](#guides/reference_building_water).

## Lead in old houses

- Canada allowed lead pipe until 1975 and lead solder until 1986. A lead service line is a soft, greyish-black metal you can scrape with a knife (Health Canada lead).
- Brass and chrome-plated brass taps and lead-soldered plumbing are the common sources; the longer water sits in the pipes, the more lead it picks up (EPA lead). Hot water draws out more lead than cold (Health Canada lead), and boiling doesn't remove lead (EPA lead).
- So the water you drain from the pipes of an old house, after days of standing, can hold more lead the longer it has sat (EPA lead). Skin doesn't absorb lead from water, so washing in it is fine (EPA lead). Children, infants and unborn babies are the most at risk (Health Canada lead): give them your best stored water and use pipe water from an old house for washing and flushing, or through a filter certified for lead ([Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters)).
- Health Canada's flushing advice (run the tap until it's cold, about a minute) needs running water, which you won't have with the main shut, and its lasting fix is replacing the lead pipe (Health Canada lead).
- A garden hose can leach lead and other chemicals into water, more so when warm, unless it is certified for drinking water (NSF/ANSI 61 and 372) (Cleveland Water hose). Drain the water heater into a pot under the valve, or through a short drinking-water hose.

See the [lead](#browse/hazards/lead) card.

## The water heater

- **Electric:** switch it off at its breaker. The elements burn out if they are powered when not fully under water, so it stays off until the tank is full again (Bradford White). Electric heaters sold in Canada are factory-set to 60 °C (140 °F), which scalds in 5 seconds (Bradford White): a switched-off tank is still full of hot water (WSC winterizing), so let it cool before you drain it, or drain slowly with gloves on.
- **Gas:** put the pilot out; the federal guide leaves relighting to the gas supplier (Winter power failures). With no supplier to call, the rule that matters is never to turn the gas or power on while the tank is empty: fill it first (FEMA 2004, OSU BAE-1519). See [Gas at a damaged house](#guides/safety_natural_gas).
- **Draining:** close the cold supply valve, fit a hose or a pot to the drain valve at the bottom, open it, then open a hot tap so air can get in (Bradford White). [Water heater teardown](#guides/teardown_water_heater) covers stuck drain valves, sediment and the magnesium anode.
- **Coming back:** a hot-water system left unused for two weeks or more can build up hydrogen, which is extremely flammable. Run the kitchen hot tap for several minutes before using any appliance on the hot water, with no smoking or flame near it; a sound like air escaping is the sign (Bradford White).

## Antifreeze: which kind and how much

| Antifreeze | Where it can go | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| RV or plumbing antifreeze, propylene glycol | Drain traps, toilets, floor drains | Considered safe for wells and septic systems (WSC winterizing). Not harmful in small amounts if swallowed, but still not for the water supply pipes (Purdue PrepNote). |
| RV antifreeze, ethanol-based | Not for traps | Less than 32 % ethanol, and a flammable liquid (Prestone SDS 834). WSC says alcohol-based products evaporate too quickly to be effective and calls for propylene glycol (WSC winterizing). |
| Car antifreeze, ethylene glycol | Nowhere in a house | Not safe in any part of a home water system (Purdue PrepNote); toxic, and its maker says not to bring it indoors (WSC winterizing). |

Read the label for "propylene glycol" and dilute only as the label says (WSC winterizing).

| Where | How much |
|---|---|
| Each sink, basin and tub trap | At least 1 L (1 US qt) of the mixed solution, poured slowly (WSC winterizing). Purdue's figure is lower: as much as the trap holds, 0.5 to 1 L (1 pint to 1 quart) (Purdue PrepNote) |
| Showers, washtubs and floor drains | Purdue lists them with the other traps: as much as the trap holds (Purdue PrepNote) |
| Each toilet | Sponge the bowl dry, at least 4 L (1 US gal) of mixed solution into the empty tank, then flush (WSC winterizing) |
| Main house trap, if there is one | About 1 L (WSC winterizing) |

Two toilets and eight traps take at least 16 L of mixed antifreeze. Don't forget floor drains and any sump (Purdue PrepNote). RVs and trailers: [Live in an RV](#guides/skill_winter_rv).

## Wells, pressure tanks and softeners

- Switch the well pump off at its own breaker and leave the main on, so nobody restarts the pump by mistake; then, only once you've proved the wires dead with a meter, unplug or disconnect the pump's wiring as a second guard (WSC winterizing). Submersible pump motors are standard at 230 V, more than one disconnect may feed the system, and some controls hold a lethal charge for 5 minutes after the power is off (Franklin AIM). Then drain the pressure tank (Purdue PrepNote).
- A pump in a deep well you can't reach won't freeze: the depth protects it. A shallow well with a jet pump above ground needs its lines disconnected over a bucket and the pump drained as its maker says (WSC winterizing).
- If you have a generator, it can run the pump to fill containers first, but only through an approved transfer panel; never plug a generator into a wall outlet (Get Prepared outages). Run it outdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from any home or building and well away from doors and windows (Get Prepared outages, Winter power failures): the exhaust is carbon monoxide ([carbon monoxide](#browse/hazards/co_gas)). See [mains](#browse/hazards/mains) and [Make a circuit dead](#guides/safety_mains_isolation).
- Water softener: disconnect it, lay the resin tank on its side to drain, and drain its controls and tubing. The brine (salt) tank itself isn't harmed by freezing (Purdue PrepNote).

## Hot-water heating

This is for hot-water heating; a steam boiler works differently and isn't covered here. Radiators and baseboards freeze too. While there's power for the circulator, keep it running: moving water is slow to freeze. Once the rooms drop below about 4 °C (40 °F), start draining (Purdue PrepNote). Turn off the boiler's switch and fuel, then its water feed valve (Weil-McLain WGO). Open the boiler drain into the floor drain and open or remove an air vent on a top-floor radiator so air replaces the water (WSC winterizing). Most heating systems don't drain completely: low points may have to be opened at a joint (Purdue PrepNote).

Antifreeze in a heating loop only if the boiler's manual allows it: one made for hydronic systems (inhibited propylene glycol), never car, ethylene glycol, undiluted or petroleum-based antifreeze (Weil-McLain WGO). Boiler and radiator water is never drinking water (FEMA FAQ).

## Appliances

- Washing machine: unhook and drain the hoses (Winter power failures), and siphon the tub or lower the drain hose into the floor drain (WSC winterizing). Whirlpool's own method needs 30 seconds of power: 1 L of RV antifreeze in the drum, then a rinse-and-spin (Whirlpool winter). Purdue says to drain the washer and dishwasher pumps and put no antifreeze in appliances (Purdue PrepNote); your machine's manual decides.
- Drain the dishwasher, fridge ice-maker line and furnace humidifier too (Purdue PrepNote).

## Thawing a frozen pipe

Open the tap the pipe feeds and warm the pipe slowly, starting near the tap and working towards the coldest part (Winnipeg thaw); water running through as the ice melts helps melt the rest (ICC winter water). Towels soaked in hot water need no power. The International Code Council's brochure also allows an electric heating pad, hair dryer or portable space heater kept away from anything that burns, and says to keep heating until full pressure is back (ICC winter water), and a health unit suggests a hair dryer too (Simcoe Muskoka). The City of Winnipeg is stricter: no hair dryers or portable heaters, which it counts as fire hazards, and no boiling water, which can burst the pipe (Winnipeg thaw). All of them rule out a torch or open flame (ICC winter water, Winnipeg thaw, Simcoe Muskoka); the ICC list also bans propane and kerosene heaters and charcoal stoves (ICC winter water). If one pipe froze, check the others (ICC winter water); if a pipe leaks once thawed, close the main valve (Winnipeg thaw).

## Turning it back on

Close the drain valves, turn the supply on, close the lowest taps first and let air out of the upper ones, and fill the water heater before it gets power or gas (Winter power failures, FEMA 2004). Refill a heating boiler to its correct pressure and bleed the radiators, lowest floor first, before you fire it: a boiler fired without water overheats and is damaged (Weil-McLain WGO). Rinse out the washer and dishwasher (Winter power failures); if you put antifreeze in the washer, Whirlpool has you flush the lines and run a wash cycle with detergent to clear it (Whirlpool winter). Open one area at a time and look for leaks, and pour about 4 L (1 US gal) of water down each floor drain that holds antifreeze (WSC winterizing). Then run the hot tap as above for hydrogen (Bradford White).
